analogy.p: Charges behave a little like magnets: like poles repel and unlike poles attract, and each one is surrounded by an invisible field that exerts a force at a distance. The analogy helps with the rules of attraction and repulsion and with drawing field lines. It breaks down because positive and negative charges can be separated and isolated, whereas magnetic north and south poles always come as a pair, and charged objects can also attract neutral ones through induced charge.

bullets: Proton: positive charge, in the nucleus, **cannot move** between objects in normal static electricity.
Electron: negative charge, outside the nucleus, **can be transferred** between objects.
A neutral object has equal amounts of positive and negative charge, so zero net charge.
**Gains electrons -> negatively charged**; **loses electrons -> positively charged**.
'Static' means the charge stays on the object rather than flowing as a current in a circuit.
The size of charge is measured in coulombs (C), but charges produced by friction are tiny (millionths of a coulomb).
Link to Atomic structure: the electron, proton and neutron model explains why only electrons move.
core.h: Atoms and charge: why objects are normally neutral
core.p: Everything is made of atoms, and each atom contains positively charged **protons** and neutral neutrons in the nucleus, with negatively charged **electrons** around it. A neutral atom has equal numbers of protons and electrons, so the positive and negative charges cancel and the object has no overall charge. Static electricity (static charge) is what you get when an object ends up with an **imbalance** of charge, and the only thing that moves to cause this is the electrons, because protons are stuck in the nuclei. An object that gains electrons has more negative than positive charge; an object that loses electrons has more positive than negative charge.

bullets: Rubbing provides the energy to pull electrons off the surface of one material onto the other; the electrons are the only charges transferred.
The material that **gains electrons** becomes negative; the one that **loses electrons** becomes positive.
The charges on the two objects are **equal in size and opposite in sign**, so no charge is created or destroyed.
Example: polythene rod rubbed with a cloth: electrons move from the cloth to the rod, so the rod is negative and the cloth is positive.
Example: acetate rod rubbed with a cloth: electrons move from the rod to the cloth, so the rod is positive and the cloth is negative.
Never write 'protons move' or 'positive charge moves' to explain charging: that earns no mark.
The objects must be insulators for the charge to stay where it is made (see conductors and insulators below).
Link to Energy: friction does work, and this energy is what separates the charges.
core.h: Charging by friction: electrons are transferred
core.p: When two **insulating** materials are rubbed together, **electrons are transferred** from one surface to the other by friction. The material that gains electrons becomes **negatively charged** and the one that loses electrons becomes **positively charged**. The two objects end up with equal and opposite charges, because the electrons lost by one are exactly the electrons gained by the other, so the total charge is the same as before (conservation of charge). Which material gains the electrons depends on the materials: for example, a polythene rod rubbed with a cloth becomes negative, while an acetate rod rubbed with a cloth becomes positive.

bullets: Two charged polythene rods (both negative) repel each other.
Two charged acetate rods (both positive) repel each other.
A charged polythene rod (negative) and a charged acetate rod (positive) attract each other.
Evidence for two types of charge is that objects can both attract and repel; one type of charge could not do both.
The effects can be shown by hanging a charged rod in a paper stirrup on a thread and bringing a second charged rod close to it.
A charged object also attracts small pieces of paper or a stream of water from a tap, but that is due to induced charge (see below), not a second kind of charge.
Link to Atomic structure: the two types of charge are the charge on a proton (positive) and on an electron (negative).
core.h: Two types of charge: the evidence
core.p: There are two, and only two, kinds of electric charge, which we call **positive** and **negative**. The evidence for this comes from experiments with suspended rubbed rods: two polythene rods rubbed with cloths **repel** each other, two acetate rods rubbed with cloths also **repel**, but a polythene rod and an acetate rod **attract** each other. If there were only one kind of charge, all charged objects would behave the same way. The two behaviours (repulsion and attraction) show that there must be two different kinds of charge.

bullets: **Like** charges **repel**; **unlike** charges **attract**.
These are **non-contact forces**: no touching is needed, and they act across a gap (including through air or a vacuum).
The forces on the two objects are an equal and opposite pair (Newton's third law), even if their charges are different sizes.
The force is **stronger** when the charges are closer together, and weaker as they move apart.
A larger amount of charge gives a larger force.
If a suspended charged rod swings away, the force is repulsion; if it swings towards a second rod, it is attraction.
Link to Forces: forces are vectors, and these are a pair of interaction forces between two objects.
Link to Magnetism: magnetic poles (like poles repel, unlike attract) behave similarly, but magnetic poles cannot be isolated.
core.p: When two electrically charged objects are brought close together, they exert a force on each other, even without touching. **Like charges repel** (positive and positive, or negative and negative) and **unlike charges attract** (positive and negative). These are **non-contact forces**, like gravity and magnetic forces, because the objects do not need to touch for the force to act. According to Newton's third law, the two objects exert forces on each other that are **equal in size and opposite in direction**, so if rod A pushes rod B to the right with 0.01 N, rod B pushes rod A to the left with 0.01 N, even if the rods have different charges.

bullets: Conductors have free (delocalised) electrons that can move, so charge can flow through them.
Insulators have no free electrons, so charge produced on their surface stays on the surface.
A metal rod held in the hand does not stay charged because the charge flows through your body to Earth.
To charge a metal object by friction, hold it with an insulating handle.
The human body can conduct charge to Earth; the Earth is a very large conductor that can supply or take electrons.
Moist air conducts a little, so static effects are weaker on humid days.
Link to Electricity: conductors allow current to flow because they contain free electrons.
core.h: Conductors, insulators and why only insulators hold charge
core.p: In a **conductor** (such as a metal), some electrons are free to move through the whole object, so any extra charge spreads out and can flow away. In an **insulator** (such as plastic, polythene, acetate or dry cloth), the electrons are held tightly in the atoms and cannot move through the material, so charge stays where it was made. This is why plastic rods become charged by rubbing but a metal rod held in the hand does not: the charge on the metal flows through the person to the Earth. A metal object can be charged if it is held with an insulating handle, so the charge cannot escape.

bullets: The charged balloon does not touch the wall at first; it only induces an opposite charge on the nearest surface.
The nearest charge on the wall is **opposite** to the balloon's charge, so it is attracted.
The nearer unlike charges attract more strongly than the further like charges repel, so the net force is attraction.
In a conductor the electrons move over larger distances; in an insulator they only shift slightly within atoms.
This is why a charged rod can pick up small pieces of paper and why a rubbed balloon sticks to a wall or hair.
The balloon eventually falls off because the charge gradually leaks away into the air.
Never say the balloon is 'attracted because the wall is positive'; the wall is neutral overall.
core.h: Induced charge: why charged objects attract neutral ones
core.p: A charged object can attract a **neutral** object, for example a rubbed balloon sticking to a wall. When the negatively charged balloon is brought close to the neutral wall, the negative charges in the surface of the wall are pushed slightly away and the positive charges are left nearer to the balloon. The surface of the wall nearest the balloon therefore has an **induced positive charge** that attracts the balloon. Because the unlike charges are closer than the like charges, the attraction is slightly stronger than the repulsion, giving a net attractive force. In a neutral conductor, free electrons move to the far side; in an insulator, the electrons shift slightly within their atoms.

bullets: Earthing = providing a conducting path to the Earth so that charge can flow away and the object becomes neutral.
A negatively charged object loses its extra electrons to Earth.
A positively charged object gains electrons from Earth to become neutral.
During the flow, a small current flows for a short time; charge = current x time (Q = I t).
The Earth acts as a huge reservoir of electrons, so its own charge does not change noticeably.
Earthing straps and bonding wires are used when refuelling aircraft and lorries to prevent sparks.
Link to Electricity: the earth wire in a mains plug is a safety wire that carries current to Earth if a fault occurs.
core.p: If a charged conductor is connected to the Earth by a conducting path, charge flows and the object becomes neutral. This is called **earthing**. If the object is negative, the extra electrons flow through the earth connection to the Earth. If the object is positive, electrons flow from the Earth up to the object to neutralise it. The Earth is so large that it can give or take a very large number of electrons without any noticeable change. Earthing is used to prevent dangerous build-ups of static charge, for example on fuel tankers, where a spark could ignite the fuel.

bullets: A charged object builds up a p.d. between itself and a nearby earthed conductor.
When the p.d. is high enough, the air between them becomes ionised (electrons are stripped from air molecules) and conducts.
Charge then flows across the gap in a short, sudden **spark**, which neutralises the objects.
The spark produces light, sound (a crack) and heat, so energy is transferred to the surroundings.
The greater the charge (and so the p.d.), the larger the gap across which a spark can jump.
Lightning is a very large spark between a charged cloud and the ground or between clouds.
A pointed conductor concentrates the electric field, so sparks tend to jump from sharp points first.
core.h: Sparks: how discharge happens through air
core.p: If a charged object comes near a conductor or an earthed object, the potential difference (p.d.) between them can become so large that the air between them **ionises**. Ionisation makes the air a conductor, and electrons jump across the gap as a **spark**. The bigger the charge on the object, the bigger the p.d. and the longer the gap over which a spark can occur. Lightning is a huge spark between a charged cloud and the ground. A smaller everyday spark happens when you touch a car door after sliding across a seat, or a metal door handle after walking across a carpet.

bullets: An electric field is a **region** where a charged object feels a force.
Every charged object has an electric field around it.
The force on a charged object in the field is **greater when it is closer** to the charge that creates the field.
The direction of the force depends on the signs of the charges: like charges give repulsion, unlike give attraction.
The idea of a field explains why charged objects can exert a force on each other **without touching**.
Fields can be shown by field lines (see next section).
Link to Magnetism: magnetic fields are drawn the same way and also act on objects at a distance.
core.p: A charged object has an **electric field** around it. An electric field is a **region** in which another charged object experiences a **force**. This is how the non-contact force between charges is explained: the first charge creates a field in the space around it, and the second charge, placed in that field, feels a force. The force on a charge in a field is **stronger when the charge is closer** to the object creating the field, because the field is stronger nearer the object. This model explains both attraction and repulsion without the need for the objects to touch.

bullets: The arrow on a field line shows the direction of the force on a **positive** charge placed there.
Lines point **away from positive** charges and **towards negative** charges.
Lines are drawn at right angles to the surface of the charged object.
Lines **never cross** each other.
Lines closer together = stronger field; lines further apart = weaker field.
Around an isolated charged sphere the lines are radial (like the spokes of a wheel).
Between two oppositely charged parallel plates the field lines are parallel, equally spaced and run from the positive plate to the negative plate: a uniform field.
Near the edges of the plates, the lines bulge outwards.
core.p: Electric field lines show the direction of the force on a small **positive test charge** placed in the field. The lines point **away** from a positive charge and **towards** a negative charge. Field lines never cross, they start or end on charged surfaces (at right angles to the surface) and the closer the lines are together, the **stronger** the field. For an isolated charged sphere, the field lines are straight lines pointing radially outwards or inwards, and they spread out as the distance from the sphere increases, showing that the field gets weaker further away.

bullets: Force on a charge is **greater** closer to the charged object that creates the field, and smaller far away.
For a point or sphere, the field is strongest at the surface and weakens with distance.
Field lines are closest together where the field is strongest.
In a uniform field (between parallel plates), the field strength is the same at every point, so the lines are equally spaced.
A larger charge produces a stronger field and gives a bigger force.
The force on a charge in a field is also bigger if the charge on the object placed in the field is bigger.
Link to Gravity: the weakening of a gravitational field with distance is a similar idea.
core.p: The strength of an electric field is greatest close to the charged object and decreases as you move further away. This is why the force between two charges becomes weaker as they are moved apart: the second charge is in a weaker part of the first charge's field. On a field-line diagram, this is shown by the lines being closer together near the charge and spreading out further away. Between parallel plates, the field is the same strength everywhere in the middle, which is why the lines are evenly spaced there.

bullets: The field explains the force: the second object responds to the field at its position rather than to the first object directly.
A stronger field (high charge, small gap) makes sparking more likely.
In a strong field, electrons in air are accelerated and knock other electrons off air molecules, so the air ionises and conducts.
The field is strongest near sharp points, which is why sparks and lightning favour pointed objects.
When the spark passes, charge flows and the p.d. and field fall to zero.
Link to Electricity: the p.d. between two points is linked to the field in the gap between them.
Higher tier questions often ask you to explain sparking in terms of the field: mention strong field, ionisation of air, and charge flowing.
core.h: Using the field idea to explain static effects (Higher tier)
core.p: The concept of an electric field helps explain the non-contact force between charged objects, and electrostatic phenomena such as sparking. A charged object produces a field; any second charged object in the field feels a force whether or not it touches the first. For a spark, a strong field accelerates free electrons in the air so that they gain enough energy to knock more electrons off air molecules (ionisation). The air then becomes a conductor and a spark passes. A higher p.d. between the objects (and a smaller gap) means a stronger field in the air, so sparking occurs more easily.

bullets: Hazard: sparks when refuelling aircraft, cars or tankers can ignite fuel vapour.
Hazard: fine dust (grain, flour) can explode if ignited by a spark.
Hazard: lightning is a large static discharge, so tall buildings have lightning conductors connected to Earth.
Prevention: connect (bond) the nozzle and tank to Earth with a conducting wire so charge cannot build up.
Prevention: use conducting materials or antistatic treatments that allow charge to leak away.
A small shock from a door handle is a small spark due to charge built up by friction on shoes and carpet.
Some devices use static charge on purpose (for example spraying paint so that droplets repel each other and spread evenly), but you only need the principles above for the spec.
core.h: Uses, hazards and safety with static electricity
core.p: Static electricity can be a nuisance (clothes clinging, small shocks) but can also be dangerous. When fuel flows through a pipe during refuelling, friction can charge the pipe or the tanker. A spark in the presence of fuel vapour or fine dust (for example in grain stores or flour mills) can cause a fire or an explosion. To prevent this, the metal parts are connected to Earth using conducting straps or bonding wires, which let the charge flow away safely before it builds up to a spark.

exam: **Describe how an insulator becomes charged (2-3 marks)**: friction/rubbing; electrons are transferred from one material to the other; the one that gains electrons becomes negative and the other positive.
**Always say 'electrons' and never 'protons'** when explaining charge transfer: this is the most common mark lost on this topic.
**Forces (1-2 marks)**: state 'like charges repel, unlike charges attract' and that these are non-contact forces; for equal and opposite forces mention Newton's third law.

**Explain why a balloon sticks to a wall (3 marks)**: balloon is charged; induces the opposite charge on the nearest surface of the wall; unlike charges attract (and the attraction is bigger than repulsion).

**Field line diagrams (2-3 marks)**: arrows pointing away from + and towards -; lines straight and radial for a point charge; evenly spaced and parallel in a uniform field; lines do not cross; use a ruler.
**Earthing (2 marks)**: a conducting path to Earth; electrons flow to Earth (or from Earth) so the object is neutral.
**Sparks (Higher, 3-4 marks)**: high p.d. gives a strong field; air ionises and becomes a conductor; charge flows as a spark.
**Calculation**: Q = I t (charge in C, current in A, time in s); convert mA to A and write the unit.
**Hazards (2 marks)**: sparking near fuel vapour or dust; prevent by earthing or bonding with a conducting wire.
**Evidence for two types of charge**: rods can both attract and repel; use 'repel' for like and 'attract' for unlike and name both.
**6-mark questions**: link atom model, electron transfer, signs of charge, forces, and fields in a logical order using because and so.

mistakes.r: Only electrons move. The material that gains electrons becomes negative; the one that loses electrons becomes positive.
mistakes.w: Protons move from the cloth to the rod when it is rubbed.

mistakes.r: A rod becomes positively charged by losing electrons, not by gaining protons or positive charge.
mistakes.w: The rod gains positive charge when it is rubbed.

mistakes.r: Charge is not created. Electrons are transferred, and the total charge stays the same (equal and opposite charges).
Like charges repel; unlike charges attract.
mistakes.w: Like charges attract and unlike charges repel.

mistakes.r: The wall is neutral. The balloon induces an opposite charge on the nearest surface of the wall, and the unlike charges attract.
mistakes.w: A balloon sticks to a wall because the wall is positively charged.

mistakes.r: Field lines point away from positive and towards negative, because they show the direction of the force on a positive test charge.
mistakes.w: Field lines go from negative to positive.

mistakes.r: Field lines never cross; at any point the field has only one direction.
mistakes.w: Field lines can cross when two fields meet.

mistakes.r: The charge flows through your body to Earth unless the rod is held with an insulating handle.
mistakes.w: A metal rod held in the hand can be charged by rubbing.

mistakes.r: The strong field ionises the air, making it a conductor, so charge flows across the gap as a spark.
mistakes.w: The spark is caused by the electrons in the air jumping.

summary: You need to know that rubbing insulators transfers electrons so objects become positively or negatively charged, that like charges repel and unlike attract (non-contact forces), how earthing and sparking work, and how to describe and draw electric fields and say how their strength depends on distance. It matters because static charge and electric fields are tested with explain and draw questions, and Higher tier asks you to use the field idea to explain forces and sparks.

terms.d: Electric charge that builds up on the surface of an object and stays there instead of flowing.
A negatively charged particle that orbits the nucleus; the particle that is transferred when objects become charged.
The charge of an object that has lost electrons (has more protons than electrons).
The charge of an object that has gained electrons (has more electrons than protons).
A material in which charge cannot move freely, so charge stays where it is made.
A material that contains free electrons, so charge can flow through it.
The force between two surfaces rubbing together, which can transfer electrons from one surface to the other.
A force that acts between objects without them touching, such as the force between charges.
Connecting a charged object to the Earth with a conductor so that charge flows away and the object becomes neutral.
A sudden flow of charge through air that has become ionised because the potential difference is large.
The removal of electrons from atoms or molecules of air, which makes the air conduct.
A region in which a charged object experiences a force.
A line showing the direction of the force on a small positive charge placed in an electric field.
A field with the same strength and direction everywhere, as between two oppositely charged parallel plates.
Charge produced on a neutral object because a nearby charged object causes the charges inside it to move.

worked.ans: Model answer: Rubbing transfers electrons from the cloth to the polythene rod, so the rod becomes negatively charged and the cloth positively charged. When the rod is held near paper, it induces a positive charge on the nearest side of the paper, and the unlike charges attract, so the paper is pulled towards the rod.
worked.q: A student rubs a polythene rod with a dry cloth. Describe what happens and explain why the rod then attracts small pieces of paper. [6 marks]
steps: Mark 1: Rubbing (friction) transfers electrons from the cloth to the rod.
Mark 2: Only electrons move; protons stay in the nuclei.
Mark 3: The rod gains electrons so it becomes negatively charged; the cloth loses electrons so it becomes positively charged (equal and opposite).
Mark 4: The negative rod is brought near the neutral paper, and the charges in the paper move: positive charge is nearer the rod, negative is pushed away.
Mark 5: The paper surface nearest the rod has an induced positive charge.
Mark 6: Unlike charges attract (the nearer attraction is bigger than the repulsion), so the paper is attracted to the rod.

worked.q: A charged conducting dome is earthed and discharges with an average current of 0.50 mA for 0.020 s. Calculate the charge that flows. [3 marks]
steps: Write the equation: charge flow Q = I t.
Write in standard form with a unit: 1.0 x 10^-5 C (10 microcoulombs).

worked.ans: Radial lines pointing outwards, perpendicular to the surface, not crossing; lines closer together near the sphere show a stronger field there, and they spread out as distance increases, showing the field gets weaker.
worked.q: Draw (describe) the electric field around an isolated positively charged sphere and explain what the spacing of the lines tells you. [3 marks]
steps: Mark 1: Straight radial lines starting on the surface of the sphere and at right angles to it.
Mark 2: Arrows pointing away from the sphere (the direction of the force on a positive test charge).
Mark 3: The lines are closer together near the sphere and spread out further away, which shows that the field (and the force on a charge) is stronger close to the sphere and weaker further away.
